clue.text: Heartless Edinburgh characters can be mercenary

indicators.note: the letters left can be rearranged into something else, signalling an anagram
the heart of a word is its middle letter, so heartless strips the central letter from Edinburgh

explanation.surface: Some people from Scotland's capital will fight for whoever pays them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' takes out B, the middle letter of EDINBURGH, leaving EDINURGH; 'can be' then rearranges those eight letters. 'characters' simply means the letters of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A hired gun is a person paid to fight or kill, a synonym for a mercenary soldier.

clue.text: Con making stink over nark

parts.note: in British slang to hum is to smell bad, to stink
to nark is British slang for to annoy, as does to bug

explanation.surface: A fraudster ends up smelling bad on top of being an informer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' in a down clue puts HUM above BUG. 'Nark' looks like the informer, but here it is the verb meaning annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Humbug is deception or a trick, so as a verb or noun it is a synonym for a con.

clue.text: Network helping one measure energy in lead-free item

indicators.note: the symbol for energy goes inside the trimmed word for item
the leading letter of the word for item is dropped, as lead is removed from fuel

parts.note: an article is an item, as in an article of clothing
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Some new unleaded product has an energy grid built into it for measurement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead-free' drops the first letter of ARTICLE, leaving RTICLE, and 'in' puts E inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A reticle is the grid of fine lines in an eyepiece used for measuring or sighting, so a network that aids measurement.

clue.text: Reckless types might set up a drink with salesmen and journalist

indicators.note: in a down clue set up means lifted from bottom to top, so the whole string is read backwards

parts.note: soda is a drink
reps are sales representatives
ED is the usual short form for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: Wild characters might order a drink for some salesmen and a reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' turns the whole string SODAREPSED backwards to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Desperados are reckless outlaws, people willing to take any risk.

clue.text: Where you may well be, initially, at back of souk

definitions.text: Where you may well be, initially, at back of souk

parts.words: Where you may well be, initially, at back of souk
parts.note: the country a British reader is likely in; its initials are the last two letters of the word souk

explanation.surface: A traveller in a market is told their whereabouts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times is read mostly in Britain, so that is where you may well be; its initials U and K sit at the back of 'souk'.
explanation.definitionFit: The country is where a reader of a British newspaper is likely to be, and its two initials end the word souk.

clue.text: Tempting dish from mess divorced man tucked into

indicators.note: one piece is put inside the other, as food is tucked into

parts.note: being in a spot means being in a mess or difficulty
an ex is a former spouse

explanation.surface: An ex-husband eats a tasty meal straight out of the mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish' reads as food, which suits 'mess' as a military canteen, but it is slang for an attractive person, and 'mess' is a spot of trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Dish is slang for an attractive person, and a sexpot is someone who is alluring.

clue.text: Fit up place for Napoleon

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: fit means able, capable

explanation.surface: A fitted-up spot for the French emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ABLE backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon was exiled to the Mediterranean island of Elba in 1814.

clue.text: In particular miss opening

indicators.note: the word for miss goes in the word for particular

parts.note: a pet subject is one's particular one, a favourite
to lack something is to miss it

explanation.surface: A specific young lady's first night at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'miss' looks like a young woman, but it is the verb meaning to lack; 'particular' is the noun sense of a favourite, a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: A placket is a slit or opening in a garment, such as at the top of a skirt.

clue.text: The tube fare?

parts.note: not the price of a London Underground ticket but food eaten in front of the television, the tube

explanation.walkthrough: 'The tube' suggests the London Underground and 'fare' its ticket price, but the tube is also slang for television, and fare is food.
explanation.definitionFit: A ready meal eaten in front of the television is food for viewers of the tube.

clue.text: Catty type's returned this clever 15

indicators.note: the word for the cat is sent back, reading the other way

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A cat has brought back a smart remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns TOM backwards. 15 is the answer to 15-across, a remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A mot is a witty saying, a clever remark, as in bon mot.

clue.text: Where one may see call girl with hair put up?

definitions.text: Where one may see call girl

parts.note: a switch is a tress of false hair
to board someone is to put them up as a lodger

explanation.surface: A prostitute visits somewhere with her hair pinned up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'call girl' suggests a prostitute but means a telephone operator, who sat at the exchange.
explanation.definitionFit: Telephone operators, often women, worked at a board routing calls, so that is where one would be seen.

clue.text: Grouchily test out feature of car, automatic one?

indicators.note: out signals letters in disorder, as in sorts that are out

explanation.surface: Someone grumpily puts a car through its test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the thirteen letters of GROUCHILY TEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A courtesy light is the interior lamp in a car that switches on automatically when a door opens.

clue.text: Book of stories is moving about cruel men in America

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go inside the abbreviation for America

parts.note: US is the United States of America

indicators.note: letters moving about are rearranged

explanation.surface: A book of tales is upsetting brutal men in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving about' rearranges CRUEL MEN to NCLEREM, and 'in' places it inside US.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Remus is a collection of folk tales by Joel Chandler Harris, a book of stories.

clue.text: Like answer, short sort

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a kind is a sort

explanation.surface: A brief reply resembling a curt type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts the last letter from KIND, giving KIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Akin means similar to, alike, so it can replace like as an adjective.

clue.text: Vision of one with head in clouds?

definitions.text: Vision of one with head in clouds?

parts.words: Vision of one with head in clouds?
parts.note: not a dreamer's fancy but the watchful gaze of someone studying the sky for signs of rain

explanation.walkthrough: 'head in clouds' suggests a daydreamer, but here it is someone looking up at the sky to forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping a weather eye means watching the sky, a vigilant look for changes.

clue.text: Part of British Army flag, say

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army
to flag something is to mark it

explanation.surface: A piece of the army's banner, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flag' looks like a banner, but here it is the verb meaning mark. 'say' looks like 'for example' but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To remark is to say something, to comment.

clue.text: Where dramas may be unfolding at three …

indicators.note: unfolding suggests letters opening out into a new order

explanation.surface: A play is beginning at three o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfolding' rearranges AT THREE.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre is a venue where plays are staged.

clue.text: Cope with being stopped by every miserable-looking person

indicators.note: the first word is plugged by the second, which goes inside it

parts.note: to face something is to cope with it
each means every

explanation.surface: Coping when everyone around is gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cope with' looks like the definition, but it is wordplay; the slang term at the end of the clue is the definition, a British insult for a sour-looking person.
explanation.definitionFit: Face-ache is British slang for a sullen, miserable-looking person.

clue.text: … as well as quickly, etc

parts.note: and means as well as
soon means quickly, before long

explanation.surface: Continuing on from the previous clue, plus fast, and the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on from 16-across; it is only for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Etc, et cetera, means and the rest, the same as this phrase.

clue.text: In the past tramp got upset about fellow sleeping

indicators.note: the reversed word goes round the word for fellow
upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so read backwards

parts.note: trod is the past tense of tread, to tramp
a man is a fellow

explanation.surface: Once a vagrant became distressed over a man asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the past tramp' asks for the past tense of tread; 'got upset' turns that word backwards, giving DORT, before it goes round the fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Dormant means inactive as if asleep, as a sleeping volcano is dormant.

clue.text: Quiet moment in comedian's routine

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet
a tick is a moment, as in just a tick

explanation.surface: A pause during a stand-up act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Shtick is a comic's signature routine or gimmick.

clue.text: In the past has dived in river in town

indicators.note: the old word plunges into the river, going inside it

parts.note: the Cam is the river at Cambridge
hath is the archaic form of has

explanation.surface: Someone once jumped into a river in an English town.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cam is the river through Cambridge; the town is in Kent, known for its historic naval dockyard.
explanation.definitionFit: Chatham is a town in Kent, England.

clue.text: Time to get one concluding offer

parts.note: an ender is one who ends or concludes something

explanation.surface: It is time to find someone to finalise a bid.
explanation.definitionFit: To tender is to offer formally, as in tendering a bid or resignation.

clue.text: End of Jazz Age covered in book

indicators.note: the final letter is covered by the word for age, placed inside it

parts.note: an era is an age

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: The close of the Jazz Age is described in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of' picks Z from Jazz, and 'covered' puts it inside ERA; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ezra is a book of the Old Testament.

clue.text: Doctor given praise excessively about odd parts of theory

indicators.note: the word for over-praise goes round the picked letters

parts.note: to adulate is to flatter or praise to excess

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters, first, third and fifth, are taken

explanation.surface: A physician is flattered too much regarding parts of his hypothesis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd parts of' takes T, E, R from THEORY and 'about' sets ADULATE round them. 'Doctor' is the verb, to tamper with.
explanation.definitionFit: To doctor something is to tamper with or contaminate it, which is to adulterate it.

clue.text: Fool is first to lie in hammock

indicators.note: the first letter goes inside the word for the bed

parts.note: a cot is a swinging hammock-like bed aboard ship

indicators.note: the first letter of the word lie is taken

explanation.surface: An idiot is the first to lie down in a hammock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first to' gives L, which 'in' puts inside COT, a ship's hanging bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A clot is British slang for a stupid person, a fool.

clue.text: Church the French found in possession of a mad German Emperor

indicators.note: the French article is found held inside the following letters
mad suggests letters scrambled

parts.note: le is French for the

explanation.surface: A clergyman and some French discover a crazed German owns a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mad' rearranges the German to RMAGNE; 'Church' looks like part of the surface, but it gives only its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlemagne was crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800.

clue.text: Hello — small daughter wanted to be sought?

parts.note: hi is a greeting, hello
D is the short form for daughter

explanation.surface: A greeting to a little girl who wanted to be looked for.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: in hide and seek, those who hid wanted to be sought.
explanation.definitionFit: In hide and seek, players who concealed themselves did so to be searched for.

clue.text: Slowly develop an idea that's no good for property

indicators.note: no good means the letter for good is removed

parts.note: to gestate an idea is to develop it slowly

explanation.surface: A poor plan matured over time for a building project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no good' removes G, standing for good, from GESTATE.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is a piece of land or property.

clue.text: Burn Her Majesty's flag

parts.note: burn is the Scottish word for a stream
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: Destroy the Queen's banner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burn' looks like set fire to, but it is the Scottish noun for a small stream.
explanation.definitionFit: A streamer is a long narrow flag or pennant.
